title: The canon
description: What the canon is, and how it is changed.
html:
Read in the Ide dialect. The original is written in Igbo; here the one term that changes is chi → si, Ide has chi: it is the word, and si / sị is how it is widely said. Nothing here is rewritten — the documents stand as written.

IN THIS DOCUMENT

Contents

Chapter 5**, where a law belongs.

The canon of Odiana — Obibi Nso

The holy book: what it is called, what is in it, and how it is changed.

1 · The naming

| term | means | |---|---| | obibi | book, scripture — the ordinary noun | | Obibi Nso | the canon as a whole — Odiana's equivalent of the Christian Holy Bible | | Okwu Odiana | the holy book; also its content | | Okwu Nso | the holy book, said in its own register |

Christians have a Holy Bible; Odiana has Obibi Nso. Christians call theirs the holy book; Odiana says Okwu Nso. Obibi Nso is the book; Okwu Nso is what is in it.

These four names are Odiana's own, and they are listed as such in decisions.tsv. They are not Igbo words borrowed for the purpose — they are the religion's own naming, which the author gave it.

2 · The books

Okwu Odiana runs to fourteen books. Books I–V, VII–VIII and XIII–XIV carry full text; VI, IX, X, XI and XII are outlines only — a heading and a few lines, with no text. That is stated here because a canon with five empty books must not be presented as complete.

| book | title | subject | state | |---|---|---|---| | I | The Book of Chukwu | creation, light, the ordering of the world, and the covenant of the earth | full | | II | The Book of Ana | the earth, morality, purity and human conduct — nso, alu, the cleansing of the earth | full | | III | The Book of the Ancestors | the ancestors, the spirit-land, the reading of the ofo, and the mandate of rebirth | full | | IV | The Book of Chi | the personal spirit, destiny, the inner self, and self-mastery | full | | V | The Book of Agwu | knowledge, intuition, divination and creativity; the call of the priest, and his consecration | full | | VI | The Book of Afa | the sixteen signs, their combinations, the reading of them, and the invocation before divination. Drafted from the the old order monograph — see afa-sources.md | outline | | VII | The Book of Amadioha | the moral law: restitution, the assembly, war, and the secret confession | full | | VIII | The Book of Rites | birth, marriage and burial | full | | IX | The Book of Light | initiation, the cleansing, and the path | outline | | X | The Book of the Priesthood | priestly office, the orders, consecration, vestments and ordination | outline | | XI | The Book of Festivals | the year, the holy days, and the calendar | outline | | XII | The Book of Wisdom | sayings, proverbs, parables and teachings | outline | | XIII | Mkpụrụ Odinana | the three pillars, and the charge | full | | XIV | The Book of Abu | eleven utterances, for first light, facing east | full |

The fourth book is the Book of Chi — and in a religion written in Central Igbo that title needs no change, because chi is the Central Igbo word for the personal spirit.

And Book XIII is Mkpụrụ Odinana — the motto of Odinana — which is the author's own title for it. This name was written here earlier as Mkpụrụ Odinani, which is not the author's word; it is corrected.

3 · What is scripture, and what is not

Scripture is Okwu Odiana. Nothing else is. Everything else the religion holds is authoritative in its own rank, and none of it is scripture:

| rank | document | authority | |---|---|---| | 1 | the author's decisions (decisions.tsv) | outranks every document | | 2 | the constitution | the order of the religion | | 3 | the purity code and the temple code | how the religion is kept | | 4 | the canon — Obibi Nso | scripture | | 5 | the liturgy | what is said and done | | 6 | the language register | how the words are written |

So the canon is fourth, not first. The author's decision outranks scripture — which is what makes an amendment possible at all, and §4 is the mechanism.

4 · The amendment register

The author's decisions change the scripture, and the changes are recorded here rather than written into the text. A religion that quietly rewrites its own holy book cannot be audited, and a reader is entitled to know what the text used to require.

And every amendment is promulgated as iwu — enacted law, published and dated — never as a recovered taboo. That distinction is the hinge of constitution.md §7.

| # | the scripture required | Odiana requires | why | |---|---|---|---| | A1 | a white fowl killed before war, and its liver read | nothing is killed. The enquiry is opened with kola, nzu and a libation, and afa answers | the reform, iwu | | A2 | a white he-goat to seal a repaired boundary | the boundary is sealed with an oblation — kola, nzu, palm wine | the reform, iwu | | A3 | animals at the shrine — "white animals, such as rams or chickens" | kola, nzu, mmanya, water, white cloth, first fruits and words | the reform, iwu | | A4 | the inner room defined as where sacrifices are made | the inner room is where the oblation is made. aja in Odiana is bloodless | the reform, iwu | | A5 | a major ikpu alu worked with a live he-goat, sixteen yams and a ram's skull | the bloodless cleansing of purity.md §8, with the community present and a period of keeping | the reform, iwu | | A6 | sacred objects activated with blood — ikenga above all | no object is consecrated with blood. "Shrines and temples are embellishments… the magic is mental" | the reform, iwu | | A7 | a second book numbered XIII, carrying the Abu | one XIII — Mkpụrụ Odinana, the author's own title — and the Abu are XIV | the author's ruling | | A8 | no standing rule of cleanliness, only cleansing after defilement | Iwu Ọcha, the purity code: cleanliness as a standing doctrine | the reform, iwu | | A9 | sacred structures left to decay — "it must be allowed to decay" | permanent, maintained, immaculate places of worship | the reform, iwu |

And three things the tradition does not say, which Odiana therefore does not claim:

1. It does not say that killing is wrong. One of its own texts calls bloodshed "not an act of violence but a sacred duty." 2. Its anti-blood doctrine is about human blood — "It was considered an abomination to spill human blood in violence on the surface of the earth" — and not about animals. 3. It has no bloodless substitute for a major ikpu alu. Odiana's is an innovation, and A5 says so.

So Odiana's bloodless rule is a reform inside the tradition's logic and not the recovery of an older bloodless religion — and every document that states it says so.

5 · How the canon is completed

Five books are outlines, and the canon cannot be completed from the sources. These are the author's:

| gap | why it matters | |---|---| | the five outline books — VI, IX, X, XI, XII | half the institutional canon has no text | | the festival calendar | Book XI is an outline and no source supplies a full calendar | | the afa sign list | Book VI promises sixteen signs and their combinations. The the old order monograph gives them as sixteen blocks of sixteen cells headed by their NABO cells, and about 150 of the 256 survived; roughly 100 did not. The sixteen code names themselves come from Anidiobu — see afa-sources.md | | the two blood-prices for murder, which the sources give twice and differently | the canon does not choose between them | | the undefined terms — a handful of words the sources use and never define | each needs a definition or a ruling |

Where a book is an outline, Odiana does not pretend otherwise. A liturgy written against an outline is a new composition, and it is marked as composed — not presented as inherited text.

Where the Obibi come from

The Obibi are thirty-five, and each one names its source at the head of the story. Three kinds of material stand behind them, and the religion does not confuse the three.

The folktales are the tradition's own stories, told as they were told. Obibi 1–19 come from the the old order and Odinani material; 20–25 and 32 from the Igbo folktale collections; 26–30 from the Uche Okeke collection; and 36, 37 from the traditional architecture of the Igbo.

The memorials are history, not folklore: 31 the abolition of 1911, 33 the women's council of the old order, 34 the mission campaign, 35 the marks that stopped, 38 the oracle at Arochukwu, 39 the museum at the old order, and 40 the masked spirits. These are told with their dates, and with the records' own uncertainties left standing rather than filled.

And every one of them is set in Igbo land. Obibi 32 was once the memorial of the water at Dunbar Creek — Igbo history, but history that happened in Georgia, in the United States — and it was replaced by The Pit at Eke Nza`, a folktale of the Igbo, because the stories of this book are Igbo stories told in Igbo places. The law that memorial carried is not lost: it is Iwu Ohu`, the law of ownership, in Book VII,

Chapter 5, where a law belongs.

The scripture names no source. Every provenance line that stood at the head of a story — where it was collected, by whom, and from which book — was removed from the book and lives here instead, because a holy book does not cite its sources. The sources are named in this canon, and in decisions.tsv, and nowhere in the book itself.

No quoted line enters this book unchecked. Every quotation in it was verified against the corpus before it was written down. | A10 | no animal was killed at all, and no blood was spilt anywhere in the religion | the Ubi alone carries one animal a year, and it is a household's table and not an altar — killed in the open by the household that brought it, eaten by that household and its guests on the day, not at the shrine, not touched to the shrine, and not killed by the Dibia. A household that brings no animal keeps the Ubi fully, and the ordinary household of this religion keeps none. Everything else stays bloodless — birth, marriage, burial, boundary, war, cleansing, remedy, and every offering at every altar. A1 to A6 are not reversed by this: they concern the altar and the rite, and the Ubi animal is neither. | the author's ruling, iwu | | A11 | A10, and A5 with it — no animal was killed at all, and no blood was spilt anywhere in the religion; the Ubi alone carried one animal a year; a major ikpu alu was worked bloodlessly | Every festival of this religion is kept with an animal killed, and so is every serious rite. Igu Aro is kept with blood, and a town brings the customary bundle — one goat, one sheep, one fowl, sixteen yams and eight kola, as the old order set the measure. The animal is killed in the open and its blood is spilled on the ground, and not poured over the altar; the altar keeps the kola, the nzu, the wine and the water. The cleansing of an abomination is scaled by the animal, as the old order had it: fowl for a minor one, a live he-goat and sixteen yams for a great one, and a cow for some of the gravest (ikpu alu). Small household rites remain light — birth, naming, marriage, sickness, private cleansing — with a fowl where the custom of the place asks for one. No human blood is ever shed in this religion, in violence or in rite: it was the spilling of human blood on the earth that made the earth sacred in the first place. A6 is not reversed — no object is consecrated with blood. | the author's ruling, iwu, 2026-09-26 |
